title: Mayy’s Two Dwellings, Peace Be upon You Both
intro: Dhu al-Rumma greets two places where Mayy once pitched camp and wishes rain upon them both. A gazelle watching over her fawn brings Mayy to mind, down to the way she laughed off his declaration of love. Far out in the heat he keeps a drowsy companion awake by singing of her. His own she-camel Saydah takes the lead, and by the close the whole caravan seems to swim like ships on the Tigris.

translation: Mayy’s two dwellings, peace be upon you both,
from afar. A man far away can love and stay true.
1.sharh: The two places have outlasted her stay. He speaks to them both as a visitor would greet their occupants, then speaks of himself in the third person, a man still faithful at a distance.

translation: May rain fall on you both when al-Simak sets,
and when the Pleiades set, a downpour that rolls the gravel.
2.sharh: Al-Simak and the Pleiades mark two seasons when rain is expected. He wishes the camps a downpour powerful enough to roll the pebbles in the stream bed.

translation: Though you have stirred an old love back to life
in a man who longs, until his eyes stream on.
3.sharh: His blessing stands even though the two places have made him weep. What the sight of them brings up had once subsided far enough to feel like a thing of the past.

translation: Yes, a sob that nearly, at the sight of a camp
of Mayya’s, cut my throat before the tears could flow.
4.sharh: Recognition catches him in the throat. To shed tears is a physical release here, the one way the sob can pass without choking him.

translation: And this when I was nearing thirty, my companions
had settled down, and judgement almost outweighed folly.
5.sharh: He had expected judgement to come with age, as it seemed to have done for his contemporaries. The little word “almost” leaves the scales trembling when he sees the camp.

translation: When distance changes lovers, scarcely ever
does love for Mayya loosen its hold deep inside me.
6.sharh: Distance ordinarily wears affection thin. He gives the attachment that persists a name used of something felt deep inside, even when it is scarcely visible.

translation: Being near never brings me any weariness of her.
If her camp moves far away, her love does not.
7.sharh: The camp and the love once had the same home. The repeated verb for moving away lets him follow one out of sight while the other stays exactly where it was.

translation: Do all lovers’ livers grow sore
as mine does at the thought of Mayya?
8.sharh: He wonders whether this happens inside other bodies too. The liver is a seat of feeling in Arabic poetry, and the verb gives an ache that one might otherwise call longing an actual sore.

translation: When a thought of Mayya crosses
your mind, it all but wounds your heart.
9.sharh: The root for a thought’s passing occurs twice in the first half. It takes only that instant for an impression on the mind to become a wound in the heart.

translation: Hearts’ desires turn this way and that. I cannot see
the portion of my heart that is yours given to another.
10.sharh: He speaks as if love could be apportioned and given away. Other people may change their gifts and their recipients, but Mayy already possesses her share of his heart.

translation: Do you know, Mayy, that between us
lie wastes where the eye can cast its gaze so far,
11.sharh: He finally addresses Mayy herself. The grammar makes her wait to hear what he does, with a whole vista opening up between her name here and the action in the next verse.

translation: I fling my gaze across the waste, hoping
to see you, my eyes streaming with longing?
12.sharh: The eye ranges freely over open country. He tries to use the very eye that longing has filled with tears to make out Mayy at a distance.

translation: By day there is groaning and bitter complaint
to her. What the night brings is harder still.
13.sharh: He can put the sounds of daytime distress into words and give them an addressee. What happens at night is left unnamed, with only a comparison to measure its severity.

translation: Some love is wiped away by separation and vanishes.
My love for you grows fresh and yields a profit.
14.sharh: Wiping leaves a blank where another love has been. In his case separation pays a return, as if the original affection were capital that kept earning more.

translation: I thought of you when a fawn’s mother passed us,
stretching her neck and crossing before our mounts.
15.sharh: The comparison begins with something he actually sees on the road. The doe stretches to look and crosses in front of the camels before he tells us why she keeps looking about her.

translation: At home in the sands, a pure-bred, pale doe,
the morning sun glints along her back.
16.sharh: Her colouring belongs to an animal at home among dunes. A line of late-morning light along her back is what the moving riders can pick out.

translation: On the soft sand, the sand of Mushrif, she leaves
a fawn. Her eyes keep darting all around it.
17.sharh: The repeated word for soft sand first gives the footing and then identifies a particular place. Only now does her watchful gaze reveal that a fawn is lying there.

translation: She saw us heading, as she thought, to where
she had left it. She draws near, then backs away.
18.sharh: He lets the reader see the riders as the doe might see them. Wanting to get back to her fawn brings her towards the very people from whom she shies.

translation: She is Mayy’s likeness in flank and neck and eye.
Even so, Mayya is lovelier, more full of grace.
19.sharh: Only after following the doe for four verses does he list what she and Mayy have in common. Naming the likenesses also lets him mark where comparison gives out.

translation: She rises unhurried. Her fragrance sweetens the tent
just after sleep, and in the morning she adorns it.
20.sharh: A visitor could know she was there by scent before seeing her. The slow movement of getting up gives the tent time to fill with her presence.

translation: Her anklets and bracelets seem to have been bent
round milkweed stems where a gravel bed holds the flood.
21.sharh: The limbs go unnamed, visible through the rings fitted round them. The plants that supply the image have smooth, straight stems and a place to grow where runoff collects.

translation: Her hips are like a steep dune over which
downpours have run, packing down its slender ridges.
22.sharh: The image calls for a dune after rain. Water has bound its fine ridges together, leaving the steep mass full and its surface smooth.

translation: Tresses hang loose over the small of her back.
Over ben-tree perfume they are wound up and combed out.
23.sharh: The length can be measured while the locks hang free. Once they are wound and combed, the scent of ben oil supplies a detail the eye cannot see.

translation: Smooth is the course her tears would take, and smooth
the waist across which her jewelled sash slips.
24.sharh: A tear tracing the cheek and a sash moving at the waist show two contours in motion. The old commentary explains that the sash has room to slip because the waist is so slender.

translation: Her earring on the fair side of her neck looks down
over a precipice, swinging in open air.
25.sharh: The pendant is the one thing that moves. Seen from its height, the space between ear and shoulder opens out like the drop below a cliff.

translation: She polishes with a twig of arak, as though
it drank Indian ambergris and musk each morning,
26.sharh: He delays telling us what she polishes. The twig seems to receive a drink of perfume each morning, like someone being served a morning draught.

translation: daisy heads that have faced the night
and welcomed the evening dew rising from Rama.
27.sharh: The flowers complete the sentence about brushing her teeth. Their whiteness is fresh from a night of dew, and the dew itself has travelled from a place he knows by name.

translation: Her front teeth are pure white, her mouth so bright
a man without speech might find words if she smiled.
28.sharh: The teeth come into view because she smiles. To measure its effect he imagines a man who has never been able to express himself coming within reach of words.

translation: She is the cure and the sickness. To remember her is grief.
Love itself would die but for this cruel distance.
29.sharh: The desired presence would quiet the very ache that keeps desire alive. At a distance he can summon her in thought, and that act supplies another occasion for grief.

translation: But fierce winds fall spent before they reach her people,
winds that score the hard earth as they pass.
30.sharh: Al-Asma'i understood these as winds that run out of force short of her camp, though they can scratch hard ground. Another old gloss sees wild animals leaving the marks.

translation: And there are ravens made to croak at parting, like
bereaved women of Nubia raising their lament.
31.sharh: The ravens’ calls take on the rhythm of human mourning. He draws on the omen of the raven at a departure and likens the chorus to Nubian women grieving for their children.

translation: They bear out my fear that Mayya’s purpose has turned
and is eating into the staff of parting.
32.sharh: The birds seem to give his private fear an outside witness. Al-Bahili explains the staff by the grub that bores into wood, doing its work before any break shows on the surface.

translation: Mayy’s husband wept because my young she-camels knelt
by Mayy’s tent, worn out at the end of the night.
33.sharh: What the husband sees outside is evidence enough to upset him. The condition of the kneeling animals tells how far someone was prepared to travel to reach Mayy’s tent.

translation: Then die of vexation, Mayy’s husband. These
are hearts you can trust with Mayy when you are away.
34.sharh: The insult and the assurance come in one breath. He grants the husband a claim upon the visitors’ honour while refusing to let him dictate whom they may love.

translation: Had they left the choice to her, she would have chosen.
A woman like Mayy is ill matched with a man like you.
35.sharh: He imagines Mayy having a say in her marriage. He leaves her imagined choice unnamed, but tells the husband directly how little chance he thinks he would have stood.

translation: Whenever I say Mayya draws near, there rise in dust
wastes where the eye can cast its gaze so far.
36.sharh: He uses exactly the half-line that earlier sent his gaze out in hope. Dust now rises into that same open space whenever he thinks the distance is closing.

translation: Mayy has struck camp. Look, there is her dwelling,
where black ravens hop and collared doves go about.
37.sharh: He can still point to precisely where she lived. Among its present occupants a black bird’s quick movement and a dove’s collar are easier to make out than any trace of the family.

translation: When I told her my love, hoping she would reward me
for my longing, she said, “You’re only joking.”
38.sharh: The reader has heard a long account of what he feels. Mayy needs only a few words of direct speech to put his whole account in doubt.

translation: She held me off, sure of her power over me, though she saw
how the love I kept inside was wearing out my body.
39.sharh: This is his interpretation of her reply. He offers his wasting body as visible evidence for an inward attachment that she could so lightly call a joke.

translation: I lie awake grieving for Mayy, while her husband
lies stretched out over what might be a dune.
40.sharh: The two men have the same verb for passing the night and utterly different nights. The dune recalls Mayy’s body as he described it earlier, now within the husband’s reach.

translation: Many a white-hot noon I have known, its heat beating down
until the very pebbles nearly split.
41.sharh: Before the traveller appears, the heat has bleached the air and all but cracked the stones. The sentence stays open across the pause to admit him into that landscape.

translation: I turned to face it with Atlal, once
the shade had shrunk and the lone, banded oryx had sought cover.
42.sharh: Atlal is a riding camel’s name. The sun stands so high that shadow has shrunk to almost nothing, and even the wild bull, marked as if it wore a sash, has found shelter.

translation: If life is to be for me, as I see it now,
torment on Mayy’s account, death would give more rest.
43.sharh: The language of relief belongs to a rider who has just been looking for shade. He lets that physical need say how exhausting the thought of Mayy has become.

translation: Many a midday this side of Mayya my young camel
passed without a noonday halt, while the dark locust kicked.
44.sharh: Even the locust kicks up its legs to escape the hot ground. The little movement marks the hour at which the camel ought to have been given a halt.

translation: In a trackless waste the very land seems to buck
in morning and noon mirage, all but sweeping sight away.
45.sharh: Seen through heat shimmer, solid ground appears to rear up under the eye. The disturbance spreads from the insect’s kick to the whole sweep of the waste.

translation: As though pure patterned silk were bound
round the hilltops, ripping open and being sewn up again.
46.sharh: One old gloss sees the sheen of patterned silk, another the watered surface of a blade. The verbs of ripping and stitching fit the cloth that the mirage keeps opening and closing over the peaks.

translation: When even the chameleon, struck
by the heat, twists its head and reels,
47.sharh: The chameleon’s turning head gives the heat a visible effect on a living body. Its unsteady motion prepares the swaying head of a rider in the following verses.

translation: many a man, drunk on drowsiness, has swayed
like a bucket on two ropes down a well.
48.sharh: At a well worked with two ropes, one man pulls when the bucket swings towards the opposite wall. The rider nods first one way and then the other, as if the two hands were still at work.

translation: I would chase sleep from him as his head lolled
like a drinker tipping back the last dregs.
49.sharh: Only here do we learn what the speaker does for the drowsy man. Drinking the last drops gives the tilt of his head a different and very exact point of comparison.

translation: Whenever he dies in the saddle I call him back to life
by singing of you, while the pale camels lean into their stride.
50.sharh: Mayy’s name does practical work on the journey. As al-Bahili explains, he sings verse about her to rouse the sleeper without interrupting the steady travel of the camels.

translation: When the ends of the whips have frayed and the mounts’
bodies thin to crescents, Saydah puts them to the test.
51.sharh: The whips and the animals carry different traces of the same hard travel. Saydah torments the others simply by setting a pace that their worn-down bodies can scarcely sustain.

translation: She has a fine pointed ear, a smooth nape,
a cheek as sleek as a bride’s mirror far from home.
52.sharh: The ear narrows to a clean point. To account for the lustre of the cheek, the old commentary imagines a woman living among strangers who takes particular care to polish her mirror.

translation: She has the eyes of a lone dark-horned oryx, a lip
like a Yemeni leather sandal, unruly when she plays.
53.sharh: The eyes come from another desert animal, while the fleshy lip looks like a strip of well-tanned leather. Its wayward movement is something the observer catches when she starts to play.

translation: Her hind leg is a wolf’s shadow. Its stride is quickened
by a splayed cannon bone, corded tight by the shank.
54.sharh: A shadow need leave no distinct footprint in the eye. He follows the leg’s speed down to the tightly joined lower bones and the slight outward turn that gives the stride room.

translation: She paces on as the black night is split
above the riders by dawn’s familiar white blaze.
55.sharh: A white mark on a dark animal’s forehead gives him his first glimpse of dawn. The party recognises the sign while Saydah continues at the same easy pace.

translation: When I call “Aj!” or start to sing, she flashes
a tail like inner wing-feathers, in calf or feigning it.
56.sharh: The command is one addressed to a she-camel. She raises a feather-like tail, a sign of pregnancy that a lively animal may also display when she is carrying no calf.

translation: You should see her after every far journey I demand,
where even Mahri camels’ forelegs have a long haul to make.
57.sharh: Even camels of the renowned Mahri breed would have to work their forelegs like arms hauling up water. The length of a journey is measured in pulls that have still to be made.

translation: Her forearms surge, she flings her middle onward,
alert to a threat, her head held high.
58.sharh: The motion can be followed from the free sweep of the forelegs to the thrust of her middle. The threat has reached her ears while her head is still held high.

translation: Reddish and tall, she makes me feel my saddle and I
are being carried across the waste by a scarred wild ass.
59.sharh: Saydah’s strength makes the rider feel that another animal has taken her weight and his. The bite scars belong to a wild jack, whose herd now comes into view.

translation: He turns his herd of she-asses, all alike, their backs
like level rock where the wild grass grows tall.
60.sharh: The jack gathers the females of his own kind round him. There is grass growing up about the herd, yet what catches the eye above it has the smooth level surface of stone.

translation: They have grazed the open country until each seems,
so lean, a straight, dark spear-shaft from al-Khatt.
61.sharh: He changes scale from broad stone surfaces to one straight shaft for each lean body. Spears traded at al-Khatt were known for the care taken in straightening their canes.

translation: Until a day came of such blazing heat
the ostrich egg nearly cracked in its scrape.
62.sharh: The ostrich lays in a shallow scrape exposed to the sun. Earlier the heat almost split stones, and now it reaches an eggshell that looks like a small pearl.

translation: All day he coaxes the mares, and they stand as though
a thirsty flock of birds had settled on their heads.
63.sharh: The jack manages the herd by coaxing it. Each mare holds its head so still one could imagine a bird remaining perched there, and even the imagined birds suffer from the thirst of the hour.

translation: On a height, at an hour thick with dust,
even the locusts vanish in the heat.
64.sharh: A height offers a lookout, but the air is full of dust. The locust first seen kicking against the ground completes the picture here by disappearing from it.

translation: See where she spends the evening. Wind plays between her
and the ground she will meet when morning comes.
65.sharh: A manuscript gloss brings us back from the wild asses to the riding camel. He leaves the night’s travel unstated and shows the wind ranging over the gap between her two stopping places.

translation: Our mounts in every waste are like
great ships swimming the open reach of the Tigris.
66.sharh: After so much attention to the shape of a foot, he pulls far enough back to see the whole caravan. Across unbroken country its laden animals have the stately motion of great river vessels.

1.1.1-2.head: مَنزِلَتا مَيّ
1.1.1-2.meaning: Mayy’s two camps. The opening vowel calls to both places, and the Arabic keeps addressing them in the dual.

1.2.5.head: نَصَحَ
1.2.5.meaning: Is sincere in his devotion. The word concerns the quality of his affection here.

2.1.4-5.head: نَوء السِّماك
2.1.4-5.meaning: Naw' al-Simak, a season recognised by the setting of al-Simak and the rising of the star opposite it.

2.2.2.meaning: Al-Thurayya, the Pleiades. Its seasonal setting served as a marker for rain.

2.2.4.head: مُتَبَطِّح
2.2.4.meaning: Of rain, heavy enough to shift the pebbles and soil of a valley bed.

3.1.5-6.head: راجِع الهَوى
3.1.5-6.meaning: “Love on its return.” An old feeling stirred back into activity.

3.2.6.head: سَفَحَ
3.2.6.meaning: Pours or sheds freely, of the eye letting its tears run.

4.1.2.head: عَبرَة
4.1.2.meaning: A tear or the choking sob on its way to becoming tears.

4.2.4.head: أَسهَلَ
4.2.4.meaning: Lets the tears run down, relieving the pressure in the throat.

5.1.3.head: راهَقَ
5.1.3.meaning: Drew close to an age, here thirty.

5.2.1.head: لِدَة
5.2.1.meaning: My contemporaries, the people born about the same time as me.

6.2.1.head: رَسيس
6.2.1.meaning: The remaining, deeply felt trace of an attachment.

7.2.4.head: نَزَحَ
7.2.4.meaning: Moves far away, of a dwelling and its people. The same verb is tried out on love itself.

8.1.1.head: قَرِحَ
8.1.1.meaning: Grows sore as with an open wound, here of a lover’s liver.

9.1.6.head: خَطرَة
9.1.6.meaning: A single passing thought, however short its visit.

10.2.5.head: مَنَحَ
10.2.5.meaning: Is given or bestowed. An early use of the root is lending a milch animal so another may have its milk.

11.2.5.head: مَطرَح
11.2.5.meaning: Room for the eye to cast its gaze a long way.

12.1.1.head: طَوَّحَ
12.1.1.meaning: Cast or fling far out, here with the eye as what is thrown.

12.2.5.head: الوَجد
12.2.5.meaning: Lovesickness, the pain of intense attachment.

14.1.5.head: اِمَّحى
14.1.5.meaning: Disappears after being wiped away. The n of yanmahi is absorbed into the following m.

15.1.5-6.head: أُمّ شادِن
15.1.5-6.meaning: “Mother of a fawn grown strong.” A doe whose young has begun to walk.

15.2.3.head: اِشرَأَبَّ
15.2.3.meaning: Rears her head and stretches out her neck to look.

15.2.4.head: سَنَحَ
15.2.4.meaning: Comes across the riders’ path in passing.

16.1.2-3.head: المُؤلِفات الرَّمل
16.1.2-3.meaning: “Dwellers at home in the sand.” Gazelles that make the dunes their habitual range.

17.1.2.head: الوَعساء
17.1.2.meaning: Soft, yielding sand where green plants can grow.

17.1.4.head: مُشرِف
17.1.4.meaning: Mushrif, the place whose soft sand shelters the fawn.

18.1.4.head: عَهد
18.1.4.meaning: Here, the place where she last saw her fawn.

19.1.4.head: جيد
19.1.4.meaning: A neck, particularly in a description of its fine length.

20.1.1.head: أَناة
20.1.1.meaning: Unhurried in her movements, glossed as slow to rise.

20.1.6.head: نَشر
20.1.6.meaning: The fragrance a person gives off.

20.2.2.meaning: Sleep, here the sleep from which she has just woken.

21.1.2.head: بُرَة
21.1.2.meaning: Rings of jewellery, specifically anklets in al-Bahili’s gloss.

21.1.3.head: العاج
21.1.3.meaning: Bracelets, explained by the commentator as made from tortoiseshell.

21.1.4.head: عاجَ
21.1.4.meaning: Were bent round to fit the shape of a limb.

21.2.2.head: عُشَر
21.2.2.meaning: Ushar, the milkweed or calotropis, whose smooth straight stems suggest a forearm or shin.

22.1.3.head: العانِك
22.1.3.meaning: A steep bank of compacted sand, difficult to climb.

22.2.1.head: هَضبَة
22.2.1.meaning: Bursts of heavy rain that fall one after another.

22.2.3.head: هُذلول
22.2.3.meaning: Slender ridges or trailing strips of sand.

23.1.2.head: عُذرَة
23.1.2.meaning: Long locks or tresses hanging from the head.

23.1.4.head: الذَّنوبان
23.1.4.meaning: The two sides of the small of the back.

23.2.4.head: مِدرى
23.2.4.meaning: Hairpins or combs used to arrange, wind up or loosen the hair.

24.1.2-3.head: مُستَنّ الدُّموع
24.1.2-3.meaning: “The course tears run.” The length and surface of the cheek.

24.2.2.head: المِجَنّ
24.2.2.meaning: A shield in ordinary use. Here the commentators understand a jewelled sash that moves at the waist.

25.1.5.head: اللّيت
25.1.5.meaning: The side of the neck just below the earring.

25.2.2.head: هَلَك
25.2.2.meaning: A perilous drop, here the space beneath a dangling earring.

25.2.4.head: نَفنَف
25.2.4.meaning: A depth of open air, as between a high point and the ground below.

26.1.4.head: أَراك
26.1.4.meaning: Arak, the toothbrush tree. A small twig provides a tooth stick.

26.2.5.head: صَبَحَ
26.2.5.meaning: Is given a morning draught, here of musk and ambergris.

27.1.2.head: أُقحُوان
27.1.2.meaning: White daisy-like flowers, traditionally compared to teeth.

27.2.4.head: رامَة
27.2.4.meaning: Rama, the place from which he imagines the dew travelling.

27.2.5.head: مُتَرَوِّح
27.2.5.meaning: Coming in the evening. The adjective belongs to the dew.

28.1.1.head: هِجان
28.1.1.meaning: Pure white, of the front teeth.

28.1.3.head: مُغرَب
28.1.3.meaning: Exceptionally white or bright, describing the mouth.

29.2.4.meaning: The growing or continuing distance between two people.

30.2.1.head: أَوارِن
30.2.1.meaning: Vigorous and ranging widely. Al-Asma'i applies it to winds, another gloss to wild animals.

30.2.3.head: الأَجالِد
30.2.3.meaning: Hard patches of ground in which the winds or animals can leave marks.

30.2.4.head: بُرَّح
30.2.4.meaning: Violent in their passage, in al-Asma'i’s account of the winds.

31.1.1.head: مُستَشحِجات
31.1.1.meaning: Ravens raising their harsh, croaking cry.

31.2.1.head: مِثكال
31.2.1.meaning: Women mourning the loss of children.

31.2.3-4.head: صَيّابَة النّوب
31.2.3-4.meaning: The Nubians in their own heartland, south of Egypt. The old gloss stresses descent and belonging in the group.

32.2.3-6.head: قَدَحَ في عَصا البَين
32.2.3-6.meaning: “Boring into the staff of parting.” A grub eating wood from within gives the figure for estrangement.

33.1.6.head: قَلوص
33.1.6.meaning: My young riding camels. Both printed texts here have “young camels”, without the possessive.

33.2.6.head: طالِح
33.2.6.meaning: Worn out by travel, of the young camels.

34.2.3-4.head: أُمَّن الغَيب
34.2.3-4.meaning: “Trustworthy in absence.” People who will keep faith when the person concerned is away.

35.1.3.head: الخِيار
35.1.3.meaning: Freedom of choice, here in choosing a husband.

36.1.5.meaning: Grew dust-coloured or filled with dust.

37.1.2.head: اِحتَمَلَ
37.1.2.meaning: Broke camp, taking the household and its belongings away.

37.2.2.head: أَسحَم
37.2.2.meaning: Black birds, specifically ravens in al-Bahili’s gloss.

37.2.4-5.head: الحَمام المُوَشَّح
37.2.4-5.meaning: Collared doves whose neck marking resembles a band worn across the body.

38.1.5.head: أَثابَ
38.1.5.meaning: Repay or reward love by returning it.

39.1.2.head: إِدلال
39.1.2.meaning: The freedom of someone confident enough of her lover’s attachment to tease him.

40.2.4.meaning: A ridge of dune sand, recalling the earlier comparison with Mayy’s hips.

41.1.1.head: هاجِرَة
41.1.1.meaning: The fierce heat of the middle of the day.

41.1.4.head: وَديقَة
41.1.4.meaning: Scorching heat pressing close to the ground.

41.2.5.head: تَصَيَّحَ
41.2.5.meaning: Cracks or splits apart in the heat, here of pebbles.

42.1.4.head: أَطلال
42.1.4.meaning: Atlal, a riding camel named in another of Dhu al-Rumma’s descriptions of noon heat.

42.2.1.meaning: Drew in or shrank, of the shadow when the sun stands high.

42.2.4-5.head: الفَريد المُوَشَّح
42.2.4-5.meaning: A lone oryx with dark markings like the bands of a sash.

43.2.1.head: تَباريح
43.2.1.meaning: Acute bouts of suffering, here the torments of love.

44.1.6.head: قالَ
44.1.6.meaning: Takes a midday rest or halt.

44.2.3-4.head: الجُندَب الجَون
44.2.3-4.meaning: A desert grasshopper. Its colour word can describe either dark or light colouring.

45.1.1.head: تَيهاء
45.1.1.meaning: A trackless waste in which a traveller can lose the way.

45.1.4.head: اِرتِكاض
45.1.4.meaning: Apparent bucking or kicking of the ground seen in the shimmer.

45.2.1.head: آل
45.2.1.meaning: A mirage that makes distant features appear raised or in motion.

45.2.5.head: مَصَحَ
45.2.5.meaning: Carries the sight away, leaving the viewer unable to hold an object steady.

46.1.2.head: الفِرِند
46.1.2.meaning: Firind, figured silk in one gloss, the watered pattern of a blade in another.

46.2.2.head: قارَة
46.2.2.meaning: Isolated hills or small rocky eminences.

46.2.5.head: نَصَحَ
46.2.5.meaning: Is sewn up again, as the shimmer closes over a peak it had just exposed.

47.1.3.head: الحِرباء
47.1.3.meaning: A chameleon, here seen turning its head in the sun.

47.2.5.head: رَنَّحَ
47.2.5.meaning: Reels, with its head turning dizzily.

48.1.1.head: نَشوان
48.1.1.meaning: Like a drunken man, in this case overcome by sleep.

48.2.3.head: مَشطونَة
48.2.3.meaning: A well worked by a bucket on two ropes, one held at each side.

49.2.3-4.head: رَشّاف الفِضال
49.2.3-4.meaning: “Sipper of the leavings.” Someone drawing the last drops from a vessel.

50.2.2.head: العيس
50.2.2.meaning: Pale riding camels tinged with tawny colour.

50.2.3.head: مِرسال
50.2.3.meaning: Camels that cover ground at a fast, easy pace.

50.2.4.head: جانِح
50.2.4.meaning: Leaning forwards with their chests as they travel.

51.1.2.meaning: Unravelled, of the ends of plaited whips after long use.

51.1.5.head: هَلَّلَ
51.1.5.meaning: Grew slender and curved like crescents, of the camels’ bodies.

51.2.4.head: صَيدَح
51.2.4.meaning: Saydah, Dhu al-Rumma’s riding camel, whose pace the others strive to match.

52.1.3.head: حَشر
52.1.3.meaning: Fine and tapering to a point, of an ear.

52.1.4.head: ذِفرى
52.1.4.meaning: One of the two prominences at the nape, behind the camel’s ears.

52.2.4.head: أَسجَح
52.2.4.meaning: Smooth and even, of the surface of the cheek.

53.1.2-3.head: أَحَمّ الرَّوق
53.1.2-3.meaning: “Dark of horn.” A wild oryx identified by its black horn.

53.2.1-2.head: سِبت اليَماني
53.2.1-2.meaning: A Yemeni sandal made of acacia-tanned leather.

54.2.1.head: وَظيف
54.2.1.meaning: The cannon region of the leg, the long narrow part just above the fetlock.

54.2.5.head: أَروَح
54.2.5.meaning: Turning outwards, of the lower leg.

55.1.1.head: وَسوج
55.1.1.meaning: A she-camel travelling with a quick, easy, sustained gait.

55.1.4.head: خُدارِيّ
55.1.4.meaning: Deeply black, here of the night sky.

55.2.4.head: السَّماوَة
55.2.4.meaning: The visible outline of something. Al-Bahili takes it here as dawn’s first outline. The vowel can sound like the plural “heavens”, though both editions give the singular.

55.2.5.head: أَقرَح
55.2.5.meaning: Blazed with a little white on the forehead, an image for first light.

56.1.3.meaning: Aj, a rider’s call to a she-camel.

56.1.6.head: أَبرَقَ
56.1.6.meaning: Raised her tail and flashed it into view.

56.2.2.head: خافِيَة
56.2.2.meaning: The inner wing feathers, recalled by the spread of the raised tail.

56.2.5.head: تَلَقَّحَ
56.2.5.meaning: Gives the sign of being in calf, even when she is not.

57.2.2.head: مَهرِيَّة
57.2.2.meaning: Mahri camels, named for Mahra and prized for their travelling pace.

57.2.4.head: مُتَمَتَّح
57.2.4.meaning: Scope for long pulls of the forelegs, as when drawing a bucket up a well.

58.1.4.head: جَوز
58.1.4.meaning: The middle of the camel’s body.

59.1.1.head: صُهابِيَّة
59.1.1.meaning: A reddish or tawny she-camel. Some commentary takes the word as a reference to her sire.

59.1.2.head: جَلس
59.1.2.meaning: Tall and strongly built, also glossed as stout or powerful.

59.2.4-5.head: جَأب مُكَدَّح
59.2.4-5.meaning: A stocky wild jack bearing the marks of bites and scratches.

60.1.2.head: أَشباه
60.1.2.meaning: Animals alike in form, here the female wild asses of the jack’s herd.

60.2.1-2.head: مُستَرشَح البُهمى
60.2.1-2.meaning: Ground where buhma, a wild grazing grass, is growing tall.

60.2.5.head: صَردَح
60.2.5.meaning: A smooth, level expanse, here a slab of rock.

61.2.3.head: خَطِّيّ
61.2.3.meaning: Khatti, a spear associated with al-Khatt, a port in the historical region of Bahrain.

61.2.6.head: مُصلَح
61.2.6.meaning: Trued and straightened for use, of a spear shaft.

62.2.2.head: تَوم
62.2.2.meaning: Ostrich eggs, likened in another use of the word to pearl beads.

62.2.4.head: أُفحوص
62.2.4.meaning: The shallow scrape a bird makes in the earth for its eggs.

63.1.2.head: صادى
63.1.2.meaning: Coaxes and gently manages the females of the herd.

63.2.6.head: لُوَّح
63.2.6.meaning: Lean, thirst-stricken, of birds in the heat.

64.1.2.head: مَرقَب
64.1.2.meaning: High ground that serves as a lookout.

64.2.5.head: مَصَحَ
64.2.5.meaning: Go away or disappear. Another reading has the grasshoppers kicking.

66.2.1.head: قُرقور
66.2.1.meaning: Qarqur, a large vessel. The plural gives a fleet for the laden caravan.

66.2.4.head: دِجلَة
66.2.4.meaning: Dijla, the Tigris. Its broad open reach gives the caravan room to sail in the closing image.
